title: Mean absolute deviation
keyIdea: The mean absolute deviation (MAD) is the average of how far each value sits from the mean: for each value find |value − mean|, then average those absolute deviations. Same mean can hide very different MAD; MAD measures typical distance from the centre, not the range and not the mean itself.
familyTip: With five dinner times or phone-battery percentages, find the mean together, then the absolute distance of each number from that mean, then average those distances — that average is the MAD.

visual.caption: MAD idea or mix-up? Drag each clue, or tap it then a box.

items: Two sets can share a mean but have different MAD
MAD is the same as the range
MAD is just another name for the mean
Absolute deviation drops the sign of the distance
A bigger MAD means values sit farther from the mean on average

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find the mean, mark absolute deviations, average them into MAD, compare two same-mean sets, catch mean/range mix-ups, then challenge.

kid: First find the mean of your data. Then for each value, find how far it is from that mean — ignore whether it was above or below. That distance is the absolute deviation.
Add those absolute deviations and divide by how many values you have. The result is the mean absolute deviation, or MAD. It tells you the typical distance from the mean.
Two data sets can share the same mean but have different MAD. Scores 4, 5, 5, 6 and scores 1, 5, 5, 9 both have mean 5, but the second set is more spread out so its MAD is larger.
MAD is not the range (largest minus smallest) and not the mean itself. Range uses only the ends; MAD uses every value's distance from the centre.
adult: CCSS 6.SP.5c: use centre and spread (including MAD) with the shape of the data. England KS3: find and read averages and spread. Not the same as Statistical questions and variability (flagspread) or Dot plots and histograms (flaghist).
Words: mean, absolute deviation, MAD, spread. Common mistakes: calling MAD the range; thinking MAD is the mean; forgetting absolute value so signed gaps cancel; averaging only the biggest gap.
In the lab your child finds the mean, marks each |x − mean|, averages them into the MAD, compares two same-mean sets, spots mean/range mix-ups, and practises the steps.

choices: the average of the absolute deviations from the mean
the largest value minus the smallest
another name for the mean
practice.hint: Think: average of |value − mean|, not the range.
practice.explain: MAD = mean of |each value − mean|. Range uses only the extremes; the mean is the centre, not the spread.

practice.prompt: Four absolute deviations from the mean are {a}, {a}, {a} and {a}. What is the MAD?
practice.hint: Average four equal absolute deviations — the average equals each one.
practice.explain: MAD = ({a}+{a}+{a}+{a})/4 = {a}. Equal absolute deviations average to that same value.

practice.prompt: Set A: 5, 5, 5. Set B: 1, 5, 9. Both have mean 5. Which has the larger MAD?
choices: Set B
Set A
They must have the same MAD because the means match
practice.hint: Same centre can hide different typical distances from that centre.
practice.explain: Set A has MAD 0. Set B's values sit farther from 5, so MAD is larger. Same mean ≠ same MAD.

practice.prompt: Values {a}, {a}, {a}. Absolute deviations from the mean are all 0. What is the MAD?
practice.hint: If every value equals the mean, every absolute deviation is 0.
practice.explain: All values are {a}, so mean = {a} and MAD = 0. Zero MAD means no spread about the mean.

practice.prompt: Four absolute deviations from the mean are {a}, {a}, {b}, {b}. What is the MAD?
practice.hint: MAD is the average of the absolute deviations.

pool.prompt: Why take the absolute value when finding deviations for MAD?
choices: so distances above and below the mean do not cancel
so the MAD equals the range
so the MAD equals the mean
pool.hint: Without absolute value, signed deviations sum to zero about the mean.
pool.explain: Absolute value keeps distance. Signed deviations about the mean cancel; MAD would wrongly become 0.

choices: MAD is the same as the range
MAD averages |value − mean|
Same mean can hide different MAD
pool.hint: Range uses only the ends; MAD uses every value.
pool.explain: Range = max − min. MAD averages absolute deviations from the mean — different measure.

pool.prompt: Data 3, 5, 7. Mean is 5. Absolute deviations are…
Absolute deviations 1, 1, 1, {a}. MAD = (1+1+1+{a})/4. Enter that MAD when a={a}.
pool.hint: Add the four absolute deviations, then divide by 4.

choices: values sit farther from the mean on average
the mean is larger
the range must be zero
pool.hint: MAD measures typical distance from the centre.
pool.explain: Larger MAD → typically farther from the mean. It does not force the mean to grow or the range to vanish.

choices: find the mean → absolute deviations → average them
find the range → call it MAD
add the raw values and stop
pool.hint: Centre first, then distances, then average.
pool.explain: Mean, then |x − mean| for each x, then average those absolute deviations.

pool.prompt: Data {a}, {a}+2. Mean = {a}+1. Absolute deviations are both 1. MAD?
pool.hint: Two absolute deviations of 1 each — average them.
pool.explain: MAD = (1+1)/2 = 1. Both values sit 1 unit from the mean {a}+1.

pool.prompt: Range of 2, 5, 9 is 7. MAD of the same set is…
choices: not necessarily 7 — range and MAD are different measures
always equal to the range
always equal to the mean
pool.hint: Range uses ends only; MAD averages every absolute deviation.
pool.explain: Mean = 16/3. Absolute deviations differ from 7. Range ≠ MAD in general.

pool.prompt: {n} identical absolute deviations of {d} each. What is the MAD?
pool.hint: Average of n copies of d is d.
